en.title: Animal Science: the whole course
en.short: What animal science is, how the degree is organised, its main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Animal science is the study of farm animals and the systems that produce meat, milk, eggs, wool, hides, skins and other products. It is an applied biological science. It combines biology with practical management. The core sciences are anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, genetics, nutrition, reproduction, health and ecology. The applied side covers housing, pasture, welfare, economics, marketing, ethics and law.

Livestock systems differ. They include intensive units, extensive grazing, pastoral systems, mixed crop-livestock farms and peri-urban production. In Africa, livestock provide food, income, manure, traction and savings, so animal science sits between biology, business and rural livelihoods.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Awards and lengths differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer a five-year bachelor’s degree in animal science or agriculture under National Universities Commission benchmarks. Polytechnics under the National Board for Technical Education award ND and HND qualifications. In the UK, a BSc is commonly three years; in the US, a bachelor’s is commonly four. Master’s degrees are commonly one to two years and end with a dissertation. Always check your own handbook and the current regulator, because names, lengths and entry requirements change.

The early years build science foundations. The middle years add production, health, economics and management. The final year usually includes a project or industrial attachment.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with foundations: the scope of animal science and livestock systems; classification and breeds; anatomy and physiology; cells, tissues, organs and growth; ecology and adaptation; genetics and breeding principles; reproductive biology; biochemistry and metabolism; mathematics and statistics; and feed and forage crops.

The core then applies these: animal nutrition and feeds; nutrient requirements and feed formulation; diseases and internal parasites; ectoparasites, vectors and pests; prevention, hygiene and quarantine; reproductive physiology and breeding management; reproductive technologies; selection and genetic improvement; production systems by species; dairy husbandry; egg, poultry and small ruminant production; swine and rabbit production; housing and farm infrastructure; pasture, range and grazing; environment and welfare; meat production, slaughter and meat hygiene; wool, hides, skins and other products; economics, records and budgets; marketing, trade and cooperatives; ethics, law and professional practice; and research methods with the final project.

Master’s work deepens genetics and genomics, ruminant and monogastric nutrition, reproductive biotechnology, and livestock systems modelling, ending with a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by linking structure to function. Draw an organ, label it, then explain what it does. For nutrition, work numerical problems and carry the units through every step. For genetics, solve crosses and check ratios. For health, learn the signs, causes, prevention and treatment of common conditions, and know when to call a veterinarian.

Use farm visits, abattoir visits, case studies and records. Keep a glossary of breeds, feeds, diseases and technical terms. Read official sources for laws, standards and drug use. Check every calculation twice, especially feed formulation and budgets. Form a study group and explain topics aloud; teaching exposes gaps. Use past questions to practise timing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
Students memorise lists without understanding. They confuse feed with nutrient, crude protein with digestible protein, and as-fed values with dry-matter values. They ignore units in feed formulation. They diagnose a disease from one sign. They treat one country’s regulations as universal. They neglect records and economics, so a technically sound farm still loses money. They also trust old notes instead of current official guidance.

In genetics, do not confuse a breed with a species or a strain with a breed. In welfare, do not judge animal comfort only by human feelings; use behaviour, health and performance measures.

keyPoints: Animal science applies biology and management to produce food, fibre and other products from farm animals.
Degree names and lengths differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and regulator.
The course moves from anatomy, genetics, nutrition and reproduction to health, production systems, economics and welfare.
Learn calculations with units, especially feed formulation and budgets, and check every step.
Disease control depends on prevention, hygiene and quarantine, not only treatment.
Keep records and use current official sources for laws, standards and drug use.

en.title: Animal Science: Scope, Livestock Systems and the Industry
en.short: Scope of animal science, why livestock matter, production systems and the animal agriculture value chain.

sections.heading: What animal science covers
sections.text: Animal science is the study of farm animals and their products. It brings together breeding and genetics, nutrition and feeds, health and welfare, reproduction, housing, products, economics and marketing. It asks how animals convert feed and land into food, income and other benefits, and how to manage them sustainably. Livestock are domesticated animals kept for food, work, fibre, manure or savings. They supply protein and micronutrients, cash, manure and traction, and they carry cultural value. These roles vary by place and income.

sections.heading: Production systems
sections.text:
Four broad systems are useful. Pastoral systems depend mainly on livestock; herders move to find water and pasture, often in dry rangelands. Agro-pastoral systems combine crops with livestock, and some animals may move. Mixed crop-livestock systems keep crops and animals on the same farm, using manure, draught power and crop residues. Intensive systems confine animals, use high inputs and aim at markets. Extensive systems rely mainly on natural pasture; intensive systems rely more on cultivated feed and housing.

The labels are guides, not strict boxes. Many farms combine types, and a household may keep a few goats while growing millet, then sell one animal when cash is needed. Land, climate, labour, capital and market access shape the choice.

sections.heading: Industry structure
sections.text:
Animal agriculture is a value chain. Input suppliers provide feed, drugs, breeding stock and equipment. Producers keep animals. Processors slaughter, handle milk, tan hides or pack products. Traders, transporters and retailers move goods to consumers. Support services include veterinarians, extension officers, credit and research. In many African countries formal and informal markets coexist, and live animal trade is important.

Case: Amina in northern Nigeria keeps goats and grows millet. She sells a goat for school fees, uses manure on her field, and buys feed when pasture is short. Her farm is mixed crop-livestock. The buyer may be a local trader rather than a supermarket, showing how production, trade and support services connect.

keyPoints: Animal science covers the breeding, nutrition, health, reproduction, housing, products, economics and welfare of farm animals.
Livestock provide food, income, manure, traction, savings and cultural value, and their roles vary by place.
Pastoral, agro-pastoral, mixed crop-livestock and intensive systems differ in mobility, land use, inputs and market orientation.
Most farms combine systems rather than fit one label exactly.
The livestock industry is a value chain from input suppliers and producers to processors, traders, retailers and consumers.
Formal and informal markets often coexist, so market links and support services matter.

en.title: Classification and Breeds of Farm Animals
en.short: Species and functional classification, breed, strain and type, with local and exotic examples.

sections.heading: Species and function
sections.text: Farm animals are classified by species: cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry, rabbits, horses and fish. Within a species they are classified by function, the main product or work expected. Cattle may be dairy, beef, dual-purpose or draft (for work); sheep wool, meat or dual-purpose; goats meat, milk or fibre; pigs mainly meat; poultry egg, meat or dual-purpose; rabbits meat or fur; horses work or riding; fish food. A dual-purpose animal gives some of two products but less of each than a specialist.

sections.heading: Breed, strain, type
sections.text: A breed is a group within a species sharing origin, appearance and productive traits, and breeding true for them. A strain is a sub-group within a breed, often selected for one trait such as growth or egg number. A type is a general class based on function or body form, such as dairy type or beef type. Commercial hybrid poultry are often called strains or lines, not breeds.

sections.heading: Local breeds
sections.text: Local breeds are adapted to local feed, climate and disease. Examples from West Africa include White Fulani (Bunaji) cattle, known for milk and tolerance of heat; West African Dwarf goats and sheep, small and tolerant to trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness); and indigenous chickens, hardy but slow growing. Their yields are often lower than exotic breeds, but they suit low-input systems. Names and distributions vary by country, so check local sources.

sections.heading: Exotic breeds and choice
sections.text: Exotic breeds are introduced from another region. Examples include Holstein-Friesian cattle for milk, Large White and Landrace pigs for lean meat, Rhode Island Red and Leghorn chickens for eggs, and New Zealand White rabbits for meat. They usually need better feed, housing and health care. For a small farm, a crossbreed may balance adaptation and yield. Example: a farmer wanting milk near a city might keep local cows for hardiness and cross them with a dairy breed, then select daughters that calve and milk well. Record yields before deciding.

keyPoints: Species is the first level of classification; function is the main product or work.
A breed shares origin and traits and breeds true; a strain is a selected sub-group.
Type describes function or body form, such as dairy type or beef type.
Local breeds are adapted but often lower yielding; exotic breeds yield more but need better management.
Match breed to feed, climate, market and health care; crossbreeding can balance adaptation and yield.
Check local breed names and performance figures with national or regional sources.

en.title: Anatomy and Physiology of Farm Animals
en.short: The main body systems of farm animals and how structure supports feeding, growth and reproduction.

sections.heading: Framework and movement
sections.text: Anatomy is structure; physiology is how that structure works. The skeletal system is bones, cartilage and joints. It supports the body, protects organs, stores calcium and phosphorus, and gives muscles a lever to pull. The muscular system has skeletal muscle, which moves the body voluntarily; smooth muscle, which moves the gut and controls blood vessels; and cardiac muscle, which forms the heart and pumps blood. A bone and its muscles form a lever, so a short muscle contraction produces a large, fast movement of the limb.

sections.heading: Digestion and breathing
sections.text: The digestive system breaks feed into nutrients that can be absorbed. In single-stomached animals such as pigs, the stomach is a simple sac. Ruminants such as cattle, sheep and goats have a four-compartment stomach: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Microbes in the rumen ferment fibre, and the abomasum is the true stomach. Poultry have a crop, proventriculus and gizzard. The respiratory system moves oxygen in and carbon dioxide out through lungs; birds also have air sacs. The diaphragm helps mammals breathe.

sections.heading: Transport and control
sections.text: The circulatory system is the heart, blood and vessels. It carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones and heat, and removes wastes. The nervous system is the brain, spinal cord and nerves. It senses the environment and sends fast electrical signals to muscles and glands. The endocrine system is glands that release hormones into blood; hormones control growth, metabolism and reproduction more slowly. Together these systems keep internal conditions stable, a process called homeostasis.

sections.heading: Reproduction and structure
sections.text: The reproductive system includes ovaries, oviducts, uterus and vagina in females, and testes, ducts and penis in males. Its structure supports egg and sperm production, mating, pregnancy and birth. The mammary glands, though outside the reproductive tract, develop for milk secretion. Structure and function link across systems: good bones and muscles let an animal graze and mate; a healthy gut supplies nutrients for growth; hormones time puberty. For example, a heifer in Ibadan that is poorly fed may grow slowly and reach puberty late, because growth and reproduction both depend on nutrient supply and hormone signals.

keyPoints: Anatomy is structure; physiology is function.
The skeletal and muscular systems support the body, protect organs and produce movement.
Ruminants have a four-compartment stomach; single-stomached animals and poultry have different digestive arrangements.
The circulatory and respiratory systems transport materials; the nervous system coordinates rapid responses.
The endocrine system uses hormones for slower control of growth, metabolism and reproduction.
Reproductive organs and mammary glands support egg and sperm production, pregnancy, birth and milk secretion.

en.title: Animal Cells, Tissues, Organs and Growth
en.short: Cell structure, mitosis and meiosis, tissue types, organs, and growth by hyperplasia and hypertrophy.

sections.heading: Cell structure
sections.text: The animal cell is bounded by a cell membrane, a thin lipid layer that controls what enters and leaves. Inside is cytoplasm, a watery gel where reactions occur, and the nucleus, which holds DNA, the genetic material. Organelles are small structures with special jobs. Mitochondria release energy from nutrients; ribosomes build proteins; the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus make and move proteins and lipids; lysosomes digest waste. Animal cells have no cell wall or chloroplasts. Cell shape varies with function: red blood cells carry oxygen, muscle cells contract, and nerve cells carry impulses.

sections.heading: Division and tissues
sections.text: Cells divide in two ways. Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same DNA as the parent. It is used for growth and for replacing worn-out cells. Meiosis occurs only in the sex organs and produces gametes, eggs and sperm, with half the DNA. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together. Animals have four main tissue types: epithelial tissue covers and lines surfaces; connective tissue supports and binds, as in bone, blood and fat; muscle tissue contracts; nervous tissue carries electrical signals. Organs such as the stomach contain several tissues.

sections.heading: Organs and growth
sections.text: An organ is a structure made of two or more tissues that performs a particular function. The stomach, for example, has epithelial lining, muscle wall, connective support and nerves. Organs work in organ systems, such as the digestive system. Growth happens in two main ways. Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number through mitosis. Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, often from more protein and organelles. Early growth often relies more on hyperplasia; later growth, especially of muscle and fat, relies more on hypertrophy. Nutrition supplies the raw materials, and hormones and genes control the process. On a pig farm near Ibadan, Nigeria, a growing piglet adds liver cells by hyperplasia while its muscle fibres enlarge by hypertrophy.

keyPoints: The cell membrane controls exchange; the nucleus holds DNA and organelles carry out specialised functions.
Mitosis makes identical cells for growth and repair; meiosis makes haploid gametes.
The four main animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Organs are made of two or more tissues and work together in organ systems.
Hyperplasia increases cell number by mitosis; hypertrophy increases cell size.
Growth depends on genes, hormones and nutrients, linking later work in genetics, nutrition and reproduction.

en.title: Livestock Ecology, Adaptation and Genotype by Environment
en.short: Climate, heat, humidity, altitude, disease and feed; acclimatisation versus genetic adaptation; genotype by environment.

sections.heading: Environment and performance
sections.text: Livestock ecology studies how animals interact with their surroundings. Climate includes temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation. High temperature with high humidity causes heat stress: the animal must lose heat, mainly by evaporation from skin and lungs, but moist air reduces that loss. Altitude matters because air pressure and oxygen fall; animals born there may cope, while newcomers can struggle. Disease challenge and feed supply also shape performance. A heavy parasite load or poor forage raises maintenance needs, leaving less energy for growth, milk or eggs.

sections.heading: Acclimatisation versus adaptation
sections.text: Acclimatisation is a reversible adjustment an animal makes within its lifetime when the environment changes gradually. Examples are faster breathing, more sweating, eating less in heat, or a lighter coat. It is not inherited. Genetic adaptation is heritable change in a population over generations, so animals carry traits that suit heat, disease or poor feed. Local breeds often show such adaptation. An acclimatised exotic animal can still be less suited than a locally adapted breed, so the two ideas must not be confused.

sections.heading: Genotype by environment
sections.text: Genotype by environment, written G×E, means the effect of a genotype depends on the environment. The best breed in one place may not be best in another. For example, a high-yielding dairy breed may lead in a cool, well-fed station but lose its advantage on a hot, humid farm with poor forage and ticks. A local zebu cross may yield less in the station but survive better on that farm. The ranking changes, so a breed recommendation from elsewhere cannot be copied without local testing.

sections.heading: Matching breed to farm
sections.text: Breed choice must match the local environment. Consider heat and humidity, feed quality, disease and market demand. In hot humid areas, choose heat-tolerant animals or crosses that keep some local adaptation. Provide shade, cool water, ventilation and parasite control, and improve feed before expecting high output. Test breeds locally and check current advice from research or extension services. There is no universal best breed.

keyPoints: Livestock ecology studies how climate, feed, disease and management interact with animal performance.
Heat stress rises when temperature and humidity are high because evaporative cooling becomes less effective.
Acclimatisation is a reversible change within an animal’s life; genetic adaptation is heritable change over generations.
Genotype by environment means the best genotype can change with the environment.
Match the breed or cross to local heat, feed and disease conditions, and test performance locally.
Local adapted breeds may be less productive but more robust; exotic breeds usually need better management.

en.title: Genetics and Animal Breeding Principles
en.short: Genes, chromosomes, Mendelian inheritance, variation, heritability and breeding tools.

sections.heading: Genes and inheritance
sections.text:
A gene is a length of DNA that codes for a product and is passed to offspring. Alleles are alternative forms of a gene at the same locus, its position on a chromosome. Chromosomes are DNA-protein structures. Farm animals are diploid, with two copies of each chromosome; gametes are haploid.

Mendel’s law of segregation says the two alleles at a locus separate into different gametes. His law of independent assortment says genes on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same chromosome, assort independently. Dominance describes how alleles at one locus affect the phenotype: complete, incomplete or codominant. Linkage occurs when genes lie close on a chromosome and tend to be inherited together. Epistasis is gene interaction between loci, where an allele at one locus changes the effect of alleles at another.

sections.heading: Variation and heritability
sections.text:
Phenotypic variation is the difference among animals. It comes from genetic differences and environmental effects. Quantitative traits such as growth are usually polygenic and continuous. Heritability is the proportion of phenotypic variation in a population due to genetic differences. Narrow-sense heritability uses additive genetic variance. Repeatability is the proportion of variation in repeated records of a trait on an animal due to permanent differences among animals.

Example: if phenotypic variance for weaning weight is 400 kg² and narrow-sense heritability is 0.30, additive genetic variance is 0.30 × 400 = 120 kg². The remaining 280 kg² includes dominance, interaction and environmental variance.

sections.heading: Breeding tools
sections.text: Selection means choosing animals to become parents of the next generation, usually on performance or estimated breeding value, an estimate of the genetic merit an animal passes to its offspring. Inbreeding is mating related animals. It raises homozygosity and can expose recessive defects, so it often lowers fertility and vigour. Crossbreeding is mating animals of different breeds. Crossbreds may show hybrid vigour, or heterosis: performance above the average of the parent breeds. Heterosis is largest for lowly heritable traits such as reproduction and survival.

keyPoints: A gene is a DNA segment at a locus; alleles are its alternative forms.
Mendel’s law of segregation separates alleles into gametes; independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes or far apart.
Dominance, linkage and epistasis modify simple Mendelian ratios.
Heritability is the proportion of phenotypic variation due to genetic differences; narrow-sense h² = VA ÷ VP.
Repeatability is the proportion of variation in repeated records due to permanent differences among animals.
Selection chooses parents for the next generation; inbreeding raises homozygosity and can lower vigour, while crossbreeding can produce hybrid vigour, or heterosis.

en.title: Reproductive Biology of Farm Animals
en.short: Male and female organs, gametes, oestrous cycles, fertilisation, pregnancy and birth across farm species.

sections.heading: Organs and gametes
sections.text:
Reproduction needs two sets of organs. The male has testes, which make sperm and testosterone, plus the epididymis for sperm storage, the vas deferens, accessory glands and penis. The female has ovaries, which make oocytes and hormones, oviducts where fertilisation occurs, the uterus for pregnancy, and the cervix, vagina and vulva.

Gametogenesis is the making of gametes, the reproductive cells. Spermatogenesis in the testes produces sperm continuously after puberty. Oogenesis in the ovary begins before birth; oocytes pause, then are released at ovulation.

sections.heading: Oestrous cycle and mating
sections.text:
The oestrous cycle is the repeating reproductive cycle of non-primate mammals. Follicles grow under follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), oestrogen peaks, and luteinising hormone (LH) triggers ovulation. After ovulation a temporary corpus luteum makes progesterone, which supports pregnancy or declines if none occurs. Oestrus is the receptive phase. Mating, or copulation, places semen in the female tract; sperm swim to the oviduct.

Case: a goat keeper in Kano watches does for signs of oestrus, such as restlessness and tail wagging, then times service. Seasonality varies by breed and location.

sections.heading: Fertilisation and pregnancy
sections.text: Fertilisation is the fusion of sperm and oocyte, usually in the oviduct. The fertilised egg (zygote) divides and travels to the uterus. Pregnancy, or gestation, is the time from conception to birth. The placenta brings foetal and maternal blood close together for exchange of nutrients, oxygen and wastes; the two blood supplies do not mix. Parturition is birth: dilation of the cervix, expulsion of the foetus, then expulsion of the foetal membranes. Dystocia means difficult birth.

sections.heading: Species comparisons
sections.text: Cattle, sheep, goats and pigs are mammals with live young. Cattle usually carry one calf; sheep and goats often carry one or two; pigs carry litters. Sheep and goats are often seasonal breeders, while cattle and pigs cycle throughout the year. Poultry are birds: the hen ovulates into the oviduct, fertilisation occurs there, and the egg is laid. There is no pregnancy; the egg is warmed during incubation, and a brooder keeps chicks warm after hatching. Management details differ and should follow local advice.

keyPoints: The testes make sperm and testosterone; the ovaries make oocytes and hormones.
Spermatogenesis is continuous after puberty; oogenesis starts before birth and pauses.
The oestrous cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone; oestrus is the receptive phase.
Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct; the placenta supports pregnancy in mammals.
Parturition has three stages: cervical dilation, foetal expulsion and membrane expulsion.
Cattle, sheep, goats and pigs have live young; poultry lay eggs and have no pregnancy.

en.title: Biochemistry and Metabolism for Animal Science
en.short: Nutrients, enzymes, hormones, digestion, absorption and metabolic pathways from feed to tissue, milk and eggs.

sections.heading: Nutrients and helpers
sections.text:
Carbohydrates are sugars, starch and fibre. They supply energy; in ruminants, fibre is fermented. Lipids are fats and oils, built from fatty acids and glycerol; they store energy and form membranes. Proteins are chains of amino acids; they build tissue and act as enzymes. Vitamins are organic micronutrients needed in small amounts; minerals are inorganic elements such as calcium and phosphorus.

Enzymes are proteins that speed reactions by lowering activation energy. Hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate metabolism, growth and milk or egg production. Vitamins and minerals often act as coenzymes or cofactors.

sections.heading: Digestion and absorption
sections.text:
Digestion breaks large molecules into absorbable units. Enzymes hydrolyse starch to glucose, proteins to amino acids, and lipids to fatty acids and monoglycerides. Bile emulsifies fat. Monogastric animals absorb these mainly in the small intestine. Ruminants first ferment feed in the rumen, producing volatile fatty acids (VFAs), then digest microbial protein and remaining feed.

Absorbed nutrients pass into blood or lymph. Undigested material is excreted. Species differ: birds absorb little in the hindgut, while horses and rabbits use hindgut fermentation.

sections.heading: Metabolic pathways
sections.text:
Inside cells, glucose enters glycolysis, forming pyruvate and then acetyl-CoA. The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and oxidative phosphorylation produce ATP, the cell’s energy currency. Excess energy is stored as glycogen or fat. Amino acids are joined into proteins; surplus amino acids are deaminated, and nitrogen is excreted as urea in mammals or uric acid in birds.

Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and some amino acids. Lipogenesis makes fat from acetyl-CoA. Ruminants use VFAs: acetate and butyrate for energy and milk fat, propionate for glucose.

sections.heading: Feed to milk and eggs
sections.text:
For example, a dairy cow fed grass and concentrate ferments fibre to VFAs. Propionate supports lactose synthesis; acetate supplies milk fat; amino acids from microbial protein and bypass protein, which escapes rumen breakdown, become milk protein. In a laying hen, dietary amino acids form egg white and yolk protein, while lipids and calcium support yolk and shell.

Pathways vary with diet, age and production stage.

keyPoints: Carbohydrates, lipids and proteins are macronutrients; vitamins and minerals are micronutrients.
Enzymes speed reactions; hormones coordinate metabolism and production.
Digestion hydrolyses feed into absorbable units; ruminants ferment fibre to VFAs.
Glycolysis, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation produce ATP.
Gluconeogenesis makes glucose; lipogenesis makes fat; amino acids build proteins.
Milk and egg synthesis use absorbed nutrients and body pathways, varying with species and diet.

en.title: Mathematics and Statistics for Animal Science
en.short: Units, ratios, mean, standard deviation, sampling, probability, correlation, regression and the t-test on livestock data.

sections.heading: Units, ratios and percentages
sections.text:
Convert to one unit before calculating: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 g = 1000 mg. A ratio compares two quantities; a percentage is a ratio per 100.

Feed conversion ratio (FCR) = feed eaten ÷ weight gain. A pig eating 90 kg feed and gaining 30 kg has FCR = 90 ÷ 30 = 3.0 kg feed per kg gain. Dressing percentage = carcass weight ÷ live weight × 100. A 100 kg steer with a 60 kg carcass gives 60%.

sections.heading: Mean and standard deviation
sections.text:
The mean is the sum divided by n. Standard deviation (SD) measures spread around the mean.

For weights 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 kg: mean = 120 ÷ 5 = 24 kg. Deviations are −4, −2, 0, 2, 4; squared deviations sum to 40. Sample variance = 40 ÷ (5 − 1) = 10, so SD = √10 = 3.16 kg. A small SD means uniform animals; a large SD means they vary.

sections.heading: Sampling and probability
sections.text:
A sample is a subset of a population. Random sampling gives every animal an equal chance of selection and reduces bias.

Probability is the chance of an event, from 0 to 1. If female and male calves are equally likely and independent, the probability of a female is 0.5, and of two females in a row 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. Probability describes long-run frequency, not one animal.

sections.heading: Correlation, regression and t-test
sections.text:
Correlation r measures linear association, from −1 to +1; it does not prove cause. Simple regression fits y = a + bx (b slope, a intercept) to predict y from x.

The t-test compares two means. Suppose treated pigs gain 24 kg (SD 3.16, n = 5) and controls 22 kg (SD 3.16, n = 5). Pooled SD = √((10 + 10) ÷ 2) = 3.16. SE (standard error) = 3.16 × √(2 ÷ 5) = 2.0. t = (24 − 22) ÷ 2.0 = 1.0, df (degrees of freedom) = 8. This is below the 5% critical value (about 2.31), so the difference is not significant at 5%.

keyPoints: Convert all quantities to the same unit before calculating.
FCR = feed eaten ÷ weight gain; dressing percentage = carcass weight ÷ live weight × 100.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample SD = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)).
Random sampling reduces bias; probability ranges from 0 to 1 and multiplies for independent events.
Correlation r measures linear association only, not cause; regression fits y = a + bx.
t = (mean1 − mean2) ÷ SE of the difference, with df = n1 + n2 − 2 for two independent samples.

en.title: Feed and Forage Crops for Livestock
en.short: Main feed resources, forage establishment, hay and silage, and anti-nutritional factors.

sections.heading: Main feed resources
sections.text:
Feeds are grouped by what they supply. Grasses are the main grazing and cut forage; they give energy and bulk. Legumes, such as cowpea and centro, usually carry more protein and, with rhizobia bacteria in root nodules, fix nitrogen. Browse plants are shrubs and trees whose leaves and twigs are eaten; they can stay green in the dry season but vary in quality.

Roughages are bulky, fibrous feeds. Crop residues are stalks, leaves and husks left after harvest, such as maize stover and rice straw; they are cheap but low in digestibility and protein. Agro-industrial by-products come from processing, for example wheat bran, oilseed cakes and molasses. Concentrates are low-fibre feeds rich in energy or protein, used to fill gaps in the ration.

sections.heading: Establishing forage
sections.text: Good forage establishment starts with a species suited to the soil, rainfall and grazing plan. Prepare a weed-free seedbed, use tested seed, and sow at the correct depth and season. Legume seed may need inoculation with the right rhizobia if the soil lacks them. Control weeds while seedlings are small, and do not graze too early. For example, let guinea grass with centro establish before livestock enter.

sections.heading: Hay and silage
sections.text: Conservation stores surplus forage for dry periods. Hay is cut forage dried to a safe low moisture so it stores without mould; quick drying preserves leaves and quality. Silage is wet forage compacted and sealed so lactic acid bacteria ferment sugars into lactic acid. The acid lowers pH and preserves the crop. Air and poor compaction cause spoilage. Moisture targets vary, so follow local extension advice.

sections.heading: Anti-nutritional factors
sections.text: Anti-nutritional factors are substances that reduce intake, digestion or nutrient use, and some are toxic. Examples include tannins in some browse, cyanogenic compounds in cassava and young sorghum, trypsin inhibitors in raw soybean, gossypol in cottonseed and mimosine in Leucaena. Drying, soaking, boiling, fermentation or limiting the amount fed can reduce risk. Identify the plant and process it correctly before feeding.

keyPoints: Grasses supply energy and bulk; legumes usually supply more protein and fix nitrogen with rhizobia.
Browse plants, crop residues and by-products are useful but vary in quality and digestibility.
Concentrates are low-fibre feeds used to fill nutrient gaps, not to replace roughage.
Establish forage with adapted species, good seed, weed control and correct sowing; inoculate legumes where needed.
Hay is dried forage; silage is fermented wet forage stored without air.
Anti-nutritional factors such as tannins, cyanogenic compounds and trypsin inhibitors need identification and processing or limited use.

en.title: Principles of Animal Nutrition and Feeds
en.short: Feed classification, proximate and fibre analysis, and digestion in ruminants, monogastrics and poultry.

sections.heading: Classifying feedstuffs
sections.text: Feedstuffs are materials used as animal feed. They are often grouped by nutrient density. Roughages and forages are bulky and high in fibre, such as grasses, legumes and crop residues. Concentrates are low in fibre and high in energy or protein; cereals are energy concentrates, while oilseed meals are protein concentrates. By-product feeds come from food processing. Mineral and vitamin supplements and additives are used in small amounts. Feedstuffs may also be classed by origin as plant, animal or mineral.

sections.heading: Proximate and fibre analysis
sections.text:
Proximate analysis (the Weende scheme) divides a feed into moisture, crude protein, crude fat, crude fibre, ash and nitrogen-free extract (NFE). Crude protein is nitrogen × 6.25, assuming protein is 16% nitrogen. NFE is found by difference and includes sugars and starch. The scheme is approximate. The Van Soest system measures fibre better: neutral detergent fibre (NDF) is hemicellulose plus cellulose plus lignin; acid detergent fibre (ADF) is cellulose plus lignin; acid detergent lignin (ADL) is lignin. NDF relates to intake, ADF to digestibility.

Example: 100 g sample has 10 g moisture, 2.0 g nitrogen, 3 g fat, 20 g crude fibre and 6 g ash. Crude protein = 2.0 × 6.25 = 12.5 g. NFE = 100 − (10 + 12.5 + 3 + 20 + 6) = 48.5 g. Check: 10 + 12.5 + 3 + 20 + 6 + 48.5 = 100 g.

sections.heading: Digestion and absorption
sections.text: Ruminants have a rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Rumen microbes ferment fibre to volatile fatty acids (VFAs), make microbial protein and B vitamins. VFAs are absorbed from the rumen; amino acids and sugars from the small intestine. Monogastrics digest protein with stomach acid and pepsin, then pancreatic and brush-border enzymes; bile emulsifies fat. Most absorption is in the small intestine. Poultry have a crop, proventriculus, gizzard and short large intestine; the caeca ferment some fibre. Their main absorption is also in the small intestine.

keyPoints: Feedstuffs are grouped as roughages, concentrates, by-products, and mineral or vitamin supplements.
Proximate analysis gives moisture, crude protein, crude fat, crude fibre, ash and NFE.
Crude protein = nitrogen × 6.25; NFE = 100 − (moisture + crude protein + crude fat + crude fibre + ash).
NDF = hemicellulose + cellulose + lignin; ADF = cellulose + lignin; ADL = lignin.
Ruminants rely on rumen microbes to ferment fibre to VFAs and make microbial protein.
Monogastrics and poultry absorb most nutrients in the small intestine after enzymatic digestion.

en.title: Nutrient Requirements and Feed Formulation
en.short: Energy and protein systems, maintenance and production needs, feed intake, Pearson-square formulation, FCR and feed cost.

sections.heading: Energy and protein
sections.text: Energy is measured in megajoules (MJ) or kilocalories (kcal), depending on the system. Feeds may be described by digestible energy (DE), metabolisable energy (ME) or net energy (NE), depending on species. ME is common for pigs and poultry; ruminants also use ME or NE. Protein is usually crude protein (CP), nitrogen × 6.25. CP ignores amino acid quality, so lysine, methionine and rumen degradable or undegradable protein matter. Feed tables differ by country and species; use current official tables.

sections.heading: Requirements and intake
sections.text: Requirements are maintenance plus production. Maintenance keeps the animal alive without gain, milk or eggs. Production adds growth, milk, eggs, pregnancy, wool or work. Maintenance energy is often scaled to metabolic body weight (W^0.75), where W is body weight in kg. Protein maintenance covers unavoidable nitrogen losses. Voluntary feed intake is what an animal eats when feed is available. It rises with energy demand and falls with bulky, low-energy diets. Intake limits production.

sections.heading: Pearson square
sections.text: To mix maize at 9% CP and soybean meal at 44% CP to 18% CP, use a Pearson square. Put 18 in the centre. Subtract diagonally: 44 − 18 = 26 parts maize; 18 − 9 = 9 parts soybean meal. Total parts = 26 + 9 = 35. Maize = 26 ÷ 35 = 74.3%; soybean meal = 9 ÷ 35 = 25.7%. Check: (0.743 × 9) + (0.257 × 44) = 6.69 + 11.31 = 18.0% CP. This balances protein only; check energy, minerals and vitamins.

sections.heading: FCR and cost
sections.text: Feed conversion ratio (FCR) is feed eaten divided by product output. Lower is better. If a pig eats 240 kg feed and gains 80 kg, FCR = 240 ÷ 80 = 3.0 kg feed per kg gain. If feed costs 500 currency units per kg, feed cost per kg gain = 3.0 × 500 = 1,500 currency units. Generally, cost per unit product = total feed cost ÷ output. FCR and cost vary with age, breed, health and feed quality.

keyPoints: Energy systems include DE, ME and NE; use the system and feed table for the species and country.
Requirements = maintenance + production; maintenance energy often scales with W^0.75.
Voluntary feed intake rises with energy demand and falls with bulky low-energy diets.
Pearson square: parts of feed A = (CP of B − target) and parts of B = (target − CP of A), then divide by total parts.
FCR = feed eaten ÷ product output; lower FCR means better conversion.
Feed cost per unit product = total feed cost ÷ output = FCR × feed cost per kg, if output is kg gain.

en.title: Animal Health: Diseases and Internal Parasites
en.short: Immunity, transmission, signs of bacterial, viral and protozoal diseases, and internal parasite control.

sections.heading: Immunity and transmission
sections.text:
Immunity is the body’s ability to resist a pathogen, an organism that causes disease. Innate immunity acts at once but has no memory. Adaptive immunity develops after infection or vaccination and remembers, so a second attack is fought faster. Passive immunity is borrowed antibody, mainly colostrum, the first milk, in newborn mammals, and it fades over weeks to months. Herd immunity is the protection a group gains when enough animals are immune.

Disease spreads by direct contact, droplets, the faecal-oral route, vectors such as ticks and tsetse flies, and from dam to young. The incubation period runs from infection to the first signs. Some diseases are zoonotic, meaning they pass to people; brucellosis and anthrax are examples.

sections.heading: Common diseases and signs
sections.text:
Bacterial diseases include anthrax, which kills suddenly with tarry blood from body openings; never open such a carcass. Others are blackleg, mastitis, brucellosis and tuberculosis. Viral ones include foot and mouth disease, Newcastle disease, peste des petits ruminants, African swine fever and rabies. Protozoal ones include coccidiosis, trypanosomiasis (nagana) and the tick-borne diseases babesiosis and theileriosis.

Signs are often vague: fever, dullness, poor appetite, diarrhoea, coughing, abortion or sudden death. Diagnosis needs history, post-mortem findings and laboratory tests such as culture, PCR or blood smears.

sections.heading: Internal parasites and control
sections.text:
Internal parasites are roundworms (nematodes), liver fluke (a trematode) and tapeworms (cestodes); coccidia are single-celled protozoa. Worms in the gut or liver shed eggs in dung, contaminating the pasture animals graze. Haemonchus contortus, the barber’s pole worm of sheep and goats, sucks blood and causes anaemia.

Diagnosis uses faecal egg counts. In the McMaster test, eggs counted in two chambers are multiplied by 50 to give eggs per gram, so 12 eggs means 12 × 50 = 600 epg. Control combines dosing at the correct body weight, grazing rotation, clean water and monitoring. Overuse of anthelmintics (dewormer drugs) breeds resistance, checked by a faecal egg count reduction test.

keyPoints: Adaptive immunity has memory; passive immunity from colostrum fades over weeks to months.
Transmission routes include contact, droplets, faecal-oral, vectors and dam to young.
Anthrax causes sudden death with tarry blood; do not open the carcass.
Fever, diarrhoea, abortion and sudden death are signs, not diagnoses.
McMaster count: eggs per gram = eggs counted in two chambers × 50.
Dose anthelmintics by body weight and monitor for resistance.

en.title: Ectoparasites, Vectors and Livestock Pests
en.short: This summary covers ticks, mites, lice, flies and tsetse, their diseases and damage, and integrated control with resistance management.

sections.heading: Pests and damage
sections.text: Ectoparasites live on the outside of the host. Ticks and mites are arachnids; lice are insects; flies include biting and non-biting species. Ticks suck blood and can cause anaemia, wounds, secondary infection and hide damage. Mites burrow or graze the skin, causing mange and sheep scab, with rubbing and hair loss. Lice are host-specific and cause irritation, poor growth and hide damage; heavy sucking-louse burdens can cause anaemia. Biting flies such as Stomoxys and Haematobia irritate stock, interrupt grazing and reduce milk yield. Myiasis is infestation by fly larvae, as in blowfly strike or screwworm. Nuisance flies also spread bacteria.

sections.heading: Diseases carried
sections.text: Vectors are organisms that transmit pathogens between hosts. Ticks transmit East Coast fever (Theileria parva, mainly East and Central Africa), anaplasmosis, babesiosis and heartwater (Ehrlichia ruminantium, spread by Amblyomma ticks). Soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros can carry African swine fever. Tsetse flies (Glossina) transmit trypanosomes that cause nagana in livestock and sleeping sickness in people. Culicoides midges transmit bluetongue and African horse sickness; tabanid flies can act as mechanical vectors of bacteria and viruses. Fleas and lice may also transmit agents, but their main harm is often irritation and anaemia.

sections.heading: Control and resistance
sections.text: Control combines acaricides (chemicals that kill ticks and mites), correct application by dip, spray or pour-on, pasture management, traps and integrated pest management (IPM). Rotational grazing and spelling let pasture rest; keep stock away from tick habitats and remove manure where flies breed. Tsetse control uses insecticide-treated traps and targets with attractants. Use full label doses, treat all animals, and rotate acaricide classes only on veterinary advice. Resistance is the inherited ability of a pest population to survive a dose that once killed it. It grows with under-dosing and frequent use of one chemical. Monitor by counting ticks after treatment and record failures. Example: if a dip that once left two ticks per ear leaves ten after the same dose, suspect resistance and seek advice rather than adding chemical.

keyPoints: Ectoparasites live on the host; ticks and mites are arachnids, lice and flies are insects.
Ticks transmit East Coast fever, anaplasmosis, babesiosis and heartwater; tsetse transmit trypanosomes.
Damage includes anaemia, irritation, reduced growth and milk yield, hide damage and myiasis.
Control combines acaricides, correct application, pasture management, traps and integrated pest management.
Resistance is inherited survival at a formerly lethal dose and is worsened by under-dosing and repeated use of one chemical class.
Monitor treatment failures and rotate chemicals only on veterinary advice, following local regulations.

en.title: Veterinary Prevention, Hygiene and Quarantine
en.short: Sanitation, disinfection, vaccination, quarantine, biosecurity and outbreak reporting, plus roles.

sections.heading: Prevention principles
sections.text: Prevention aims to keep pathogens out, stop them spreading, and detect them early. Sanitation means cleaning organic matter from pens, equipment, vehicles and people. Cleaning must come before disinfection, because dirt and manure protect microbes. Disinfection uses approved chemicals or heat to kill or inactivate pathogens on clean surfaces; it does not sterilise. Biosecurity is the set of routines that reduce introduction and spread: fences, controlled entry, footbaths, clean clothing, rodent and insect control, all-in all-out batches, and safe feed and water. Quarantine is the separation of new or returning animals for a set period, with separate equipment and handlers, before mixing them with the herd or flock. Sick animals are isolated rather than quarantined.

sections.heading: Vaccination and roles
sections.text: Vaccines work only if stored and given correctly. A schedule states which vaccine, dose, route, age and interval. Schedules differ by species, disease risk, country and manufacturer, so follow the label and local veterinary advice; do not copy another farm’s dates. The farmer provides housing, clean water, records, and reports illness. The veterinarian diagnoses, prescribes, designs prevention plans, and checks vaccine handling. The state veterinary service sets rules, monitors notifiable diseases, runs campaigns, inspects farms and markets, and controls movement.

sections.heading: Outbreak reporting and case
sections.text: Some diseases are notifiable, meaning suspected cases must by law be reported promptly to the state veterinary service, which investigates and may restrict movement. Delayed reporting lets disease spread. A case: on a small poultry farm near Ibadan, Nigeria, Mrs Adeyemi sees several sudden deaths. She stops visitors and sales, isolates the affected house, wears dedicated boots, calls the veterinarian, and reports the suspicion to the state veterinary service. The veterinarian takes samples and advises on cleaning and disposal. The state service confirms the diagnosis and decides on movement controls. Exact rules and contact details vary by country, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Sanitation removes dirt; disinfection kills or inactivates pathogens on clean surfaces.
Biosecurity reduces the chance of pathogens entering and spreading on a farm.
Quarantine separates new or returning animals before they mix with the herd or flock; sick animals are isolated.
Vaccination schedules vary by species, disease, country and manufacturer; follow label and veterinary advice.
Farmers, veterinarians and the state veterinary service share prevention duties.
Report suspected notifiable disease outbreaks promptly to the state veterinary service.

en.title: Reproductive Physiology and Breeding Management
en.short: Heat detection, service and AI, semen handling, pregnancy diagnosis, infertility and cycle control on the farm.

sections.heading: Hormones and heat
sections.text:
Hormones control the cycle. GnRH from the hypothalamus releases FSH and LH from the pituitary. FSH grows follicles that make oestrogen, which causes standing heat. After ovulation the corpus luteum (CL) makes progesterone, which suppresses heat; if pregnancy fails, uterine prostaglandin F2α lyses the CL.

Heat detection relies on standing to be mounted, the primary sign. Secondary signs are restlessness, mucus, vulval swelling and lower feed or milk. Tail paint, chalk and teaser animals help; observe twice daily.

sections.heading: Service, AI and semen
sections.text: Natural service uses a fertile bull; watch injury and bull-to-cow ratio. Artificial insemination (AI) places semen in the cervix or uterus. In cattle, AI is often timed about 12 hours after standing heat begins, but follow local advice. Keep frozen straws in liquid nitrogen at about −196 °C, thaw them at the temperature and time stated by the supplier (commonly 35 to 37 °C for 30 to 45 seconds), and inseminate soon after. Thawing errors kill sperm.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and infertility
sections.text: Pregnancy diagnosis uses non-return to heat, rectal palpation, ultrasound or laboratory tests; the earliest reliable day varies. Infertility includes anoestrus (no cycles), repeat breeding (three or more services without conception despite normal cycles), cystic ovaries and uterine infection. Poor body condition, heat stress and bull infertility are common causes. Hormonal control uses prostaglandin F2α to lyse a functional CL and bring on heat, progesterone devices to synchronise cycles, and GnRH in protocols such as Ovsynch. These are veterinary decisions; follow labels and withdrawal periods.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text:
A Nigerian dairy herd of 50 cows is checked for heat over 21 days. Forty are inseminated and 30 conceive. Conception rate = 30 ÷ 40 = 75%. Pregnancy rate for the cycle = 30 ÷ 50 = 60%.

For a 365-day calving interval with 283 days gestation, a cow must conceive within 365 − 283 = 82 days after calving. A cow empty at 120 days needs investigation, not just another service.

keyPoints: GnRH releases FSH and LH; oestrogen causes standing heat and progesterone from the CL suppresses it.
Standing to be mounted is the primary sign of heat; secondary signs and aids support twice-daily observation.
In cattle, inseminate about 12 hours after standing heat begins, following local advice.
Frozen semen must stay in liquid nitrogen and be thawed exactly as the supplier states.
Conception rate = cows conceiving ÷ cows inseminated; pregnancy rate = cows conceiving ÷ cows eligible.
To calve every 365 days with 283 days gestation, a cow must conceive within 82 days of calving.

en.title: Improved Reproductive Technologies in Livestock
en.short: MOET, oestrus synchronisation, multiple births, semen and embryo sexing, and in vitro methods.

sections.heading: Synchronising oestrus
sections.text: Oestrus synchronisation uses hormones to make a group of females show heat and ovulate at a planned time. Prostaglandins break down the corpus luteum, the structure that produces progesterone and maintains early pregnancy; progestagens hold the cycle until withdrawal. It makes AI and embryo transfer easier and groups calving into a short, planned period. Needs syringes, hormones, records and heat detection aids. Skill is moderate: safe handling, injection, heat detection. Cost is moderate and varies with drug and labour prices.

sections.heading: MOET and multiple births
sections.text: Multiple ovulation and embryo transfer (MOET) treats a donor with gonadotrophin to superovulate (release many eggs), inseminates her, then flushes embryos from the uterus about six to eight days after oestrus. Embryos are transferred to synchronised recipients or frozen. Multiple births can be raised by selecting prolific breeds, flushing (extra feeding before breeding to raise ovulation rate), or transferring two embryos. Twinning in cattle raises the risk of dystocia, meaning difficult birth. MOET needs flushing equipment, microscope, incubator, liquid nitrogen and transfer guns, plus high veterinary skill; cost is high. Multiple-birth management needs records and ultrasound, moderate skill and low to moderate cost.

sections.heading: Sexing and in vitro methods
sections.text: Sexed semen is usually sorted by flow cytometry, a cell-sorting method that separates X-bearing and Y-bearing sperm by DNA content; it needs a flow cytometer and AI equipment. Sexed embryos need biopsy under a micromanipulator, a microscope and PCR (a DNA copying test). In vitro methods include ovum pick-up (collecting eggs), in vitro maturation, fertilisation and culture. They need a laboratory with incubators, culture media, micromanipulators, microscopes and liquid nitrogen. Sexing and in vitro work need high laboratory skill and high cost. Sexed semen can lower fertility, and results vary by species and operator.

sections.heading: Choosing a technology
sections.text: Start with records, health and nutrition. A small farm may gain most from synchronisation and AI. MOET and in vitro methods suit breeding programmes with laboratory support. Check local drug rules, welfare rules and current prices with a veterinarian and laboratory. Costs and success rates vary by country, species and year.

keyPoints: Oestrus synchronisation uses hormones to time heat and ovulation, making AI and embryo transfer easier.
MOET superovulates a donor, flushes embryos and transfers them to synchronised recipients.
Multiple births can be raised by genetics, flushing or two-embryo transfer, but twinning raises dystocia risk.
Sexed semen is sorted by flow cytometry; sexed embryos are tested by biopsy and PCR.
In vitro methods need laboratory culture and high skill.
Equipment, skill and cost rise from synchronisation to MOET and in vitro work; check local prices and rules.

en.title: Selection and Genetic Improvement Programmes
en.short: Estimating breeding values, designing selection programmes, progeny testing, crossbreeding and grading up.

sections.heading: Breeding values and records
sections.text:
A breeding value is the genetic merit an animal passes to offspring. We estimate it as an estimated breeding value (EBV) from the animal’s own records, relatives and progeny. Performance recording means measuring traits such as birth weight, weaning weight, milk yield or egg number under known conditions.

Compare animals in contemporary groups (same herd, season, management) so environment does not bias the estimate. More records and higher heritability (the share of variation due to genetic differences) make EBVs more accurate. Selection is on EBVs, not raw performance alone.

sections.heading: Progeny testing and design
sections.text:
Progeny testing judges a sire by the performance of his offspring. It is useful for sex-limited traits such as milk yield and for lowly heritable traits, but it is slow and costly and lengthens the generation interval (the average age of parents when their offspring are born).

A selection programme starts with a breeding objective, then chooses measurable traits, records them, estimates EBVs, selects the best animals and mates them, using artificial insemination (AI) where practical. Keep the breeding population large enough to limit inbreeding.

sections.heading: Crossbreeding and grading up
sections.text:
Use purebred selection to improve a breed. Use crossbreeding for commercial animals when heterosis (hybrid vigour) and breed complementarity (the strengths of one breed cover the weaknesses of the other) matter.

Grading up is repeated mating of local females to sires of a desired breed. After n generations the expected fraction of the desired breed is 1 − (1/2)^n. Example: after 5 generations, 1 − 1/32 = 31/32 = 96.875 per cent. Grading up is slower than crossbreeding but keeps adaptation.

sections.heading: Rate of genetic gain
sections.text:
Genetic gain per year is ΔG = (i × r × σ_A) ÷ L. Here i is selection intensity (how strongly animals are selected), r is accuracy (correlation between EBV and true breeding value), σ_A is additive genetic standard deviation and L is generation interval in years.

Example: i = 1.4, r = 0.6, σ_A = 20 kg and L = 4 years give ΔG = (1.4 × 0.6 × 20) ÷ 4 = 4.2 kg per year. Shorten L, improve accuracy and record more animals to raise gain.

keyPoints: A breeding value is the genetic merit passed to offspring; an EBV estimates it from records and relatives.
Performance recording must compare animals in contemporary groups.
Progeny testing is useful for sex-limited or lowly heritable traits but lengthens the generation interval.
Selection improves a pure breed; crossbreeding exploits heterosis; grading up repeatedly uses purebred sires on local females.
After n generations of grading up, the expected fraction of the desired breed is 1 − (1/2)^n.
Genetic gain per year is ΔG = (i × r × σ_A) ÷ L, where i is selection intensity, r is accuracy, σ_A is additive genetic standard deviation and L is generation interval.

en.title: Reproduction and Production Systems by Species
en.short: Compare breeding seasons, litter sizes, gestation and management of cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and poultry.

sections.heading: Seasons and gestation
sections.text:
Breeding season is when females cycle and conceive. Cattle and pigs can breed all year in managed systems. Many temperate sheep breeds are seasonal, mating in autumn as days shorten. Goats vary: temperate breeds are often seasonal, while many tropical breeds breed year-round. Poultry breeding is not seasonal under controlled light.

Gestation, the pregnancy length, is about 280 to 285 days for cattle, 145 to 150 for sheep, about 150 for goats and about 114 for pigs. Chicken eggs hatch in about 21 days; this is incubation, not gestation. Breeds vary, so use local figures.

sections.heading: Litter and management
sections.text:
Litter size is the number of young born at one birth. Cattle usually produce one calf; twins are uncommon. Sheep and goats commonly produce one or two, and some breeds produce more. Pigs are prolific, often bearing 8 to 12 piglets, though weaned numbers are lower. Poultry differ: a broody hen may hatch about 10 to 15 eggs, while commercial hens lay many eggs for incubation.

Management follows these patterns. Cattle need longer feeding and care per animal. Sheep and goats suit grazing and browsing, including community systems. Pigs need close supervision at birth and good feed. Poultry need controlled housing, light and disease control.

sections.heading: Stocking and output
sections.text:
Stocking rate is animals per unit of land. Carrying capacity is the maximum sustainable stocking rate. To compare species, convert them to livestock units (LU), based on feed demand. LU values differ, so use a local table. Example: 100 ha at 2 ha per LU gives 50 LU. If a cow is 1 LU, that is 50 cows. If a ewe is 0.15 LU, 50 ÷ 0.15 = 333 ewes.

At 0.8 calf per cow yearly, output is 40 calves. At 1.5 lambs per ewe yearly, output is 333 × 1.5 = 499.5, about 500 lambs. Head counts mislead because carcase weight and milk yield differ. Pigs and poultry are housed, so space and feed, not grazing land, set output.

keyPoints: A breeding season is the period when females conceive; cattle and pigs are often year-round, many temperate sheep are seasonal, and goats and poultry vary with breed and management.
Typical gestation is about 280 to 285 days in cattle, 145 to 150 in sheep, about 150 in goats and about 114 in pigs; chicken eggs hatch in about 21 days.
Litter size is usually one in cattle, one to two in sheep and goats, 8 to 12 in pigs, and many chicks per clutch or incubation in poultry.
Stocking rate = animals ÷ land area; carrying capacity is the maximum sustainable stocking rate.
Convert species to livestock units with a local table before comparing; LU values differ by country and system.
Output per hectare = stocking rate × output per animal; pigs and poultry are limited mainly by housing and feed, not grazing land.

en.title: Milk Production and Dairy Husbandry
en.short: Lactation, milking routine, milk quality, calf rearing, lactation curves and milk handling.

sections.heading: Lactation and yield
sections.text: Lactation is the period after calving when the mammary gland secretes milk. Alveoli, the milk-secreting sacs, are squeezed by small muscle-like cells when the hormone oxytocin is released; this is milk let-down, and stress can block it. Colostrum is the first thick, antibody-rich milk. Cow milk is about 87% water and 13% solids: fat, protein, lactose and minerals. Composition varies with species, breed, feed and stage of lactation. Yield follows a lactation curve: it rises to a peak, then falls. Persistency is how slowly yield declines. Suppose peak yield is 25 L/day and the monthly decline is 8%. Next month: 25 × (1 − 0.08) = 23 L/day. Yield depends on genetics, parity (calving number), nutrition, milking frequency, disease and heat stress.

sections.heading: Milking and quality
sections.text: A hygienic routine protects udder health and milk quality. Wash and dry teats, check foremilk for clots, attach the machine, and avoid overmilking. After milking, disinfect teats. Clean and sanitise equipment. Mastitis is udder inflammation; it raises somatic cell count (SCC), the number of body cells per millilitre. Quality tests include SCC, total bacterial count, antibiotic residues and added water. Milk from cows treated with antibiotics must be withheld for the labelled period. Standards differ by country, so check the national food safety or dairy authority.

sections.heading: Calf rearing
sections.text: Calves are born with little immunity. Give clean colostrum soon after birth, because antibodies are absorbed only briefly. Feed measured milk or milk replacer, provide water and starter feed to develop the rumen (first stomach), and wean when the calf eats enough dry feed. Hygiene, bedding and gradual changes reduce the risk of scours (diarrhoea) and pneumonia.

sections.heading: Milk handling
sections.text: Cool milk quickly after milking, because bacteria multiply in warm milk. Use food-grade containers and keep the milk cold to the buyer or processor. Do not mix abnormal or antibiotic milk with saleable milk. Processing may include pasteurisation, separation, fermentation or cheese making. Record yields and treatments. For sale, follow the buyer’s and national quality rules.

keyPoints: Lactation is the milk-secreting period after calving; oxytocin causes let-down and stress can block it.
Colostrum is antibody-rich first milk and must be fed early because absorption is brief.
A clean milking routine with foremilk checking and teat disinfection reduces mastitis and somatic cell count.
Milk yield rises to a peak then declines; persistency describes how slowly it falls, and next yield = current yield × (1 − decline rate) for a constant monthly decline.
Cow milk is mostly water with fat, protein, lactose and minerals, and composition varies with species, breed, feed and stage.
Cool milk quickly, withhold antibiotic milk, and follow national quality rules.

en.title: Egg, Poultry and Small Ruminant Production
en.short: Layer and broiler management, egg formation, hatchery, flock health, and sheep versus goat systems.

sections.heading: Layers and broilers
sections.text: A layer is kept for eggs; a broiler for meat. Layer pullets are reared to point of lay (start of laying), then housed with nests, dry litter and good ventilation. Their feed carries extra calcium for shell formation. Broilers are often managed all-in, all-out: one flock fills the house, then it is emptied and cleaned. Brooding means warming chicks. Both need clean water, correct stocking density and fresh air. Feed conversion ratio is feed eaten divided by weight gain or eggs produced; lower is better.

sections.heading: Egg formation and hatchery
sections.text: An egg forms in the hen’s oviduct over roughly a day: yolk ovulated, albumen added, then shell membranes and shell. A hen lays best with about 14 to 16 hours of light, but check breed and local guidance. Hatching needs fertile eggs, clean shells, steady warmth (about 37.5 °C in forced-draft incubators), turning and humidity; follow the incubator maker’s settings. Candling means shining light through an egg to see development. Hatchery hygiene prevents infection.

sections.heading: Flock health
sections.text: Healthy flocks show alert birds, good growth and clean droppings. Vaccination programmes, biosecurity (keeping disease out), clean water and prompt removal of sick birds are core. Common problems include coccidiosis, Newcastle disease and external parasites; diagnosis needs a veterinarian. Record deaths and egg or weight changes daily.

sections.heading: Sheep and goats compared
sections.text: Sheep and goats differ in feeding and behaviour. Goats browse more (eat shrubs), prefer shrubs and need fencing; sheep graze closer and are more flocking. For meat, both are kept; for milk, dairy goats are common and some sheep are milked; for fibre, sheep give wool and some goats give mohair or cashmere. Housing must be dry and ventilated. Common problems include internal parasites, foot rot and predation. Systems vary by country and climate; check local advice.

keyPoints: Layers are kept for eggs and broilers for meat; feed conversion ratio = feed eaten ÷ output, and lower is better.
All-in, all-out means one flock fills and empties the house, reducing disease carry-over.
Egg formation occurs in the oviduct; shell formation needs calcium.
Hatching needs fertile eggs, about 37.5 °C, turning, humidity and hygiene.
Biosecurity, vaccination and prompt removal of sick birds protect flocks.
Goats browse more and sheep graze closer; fibre is wool from sheep or mohair and cashmere from some goats.

en.title: Swine and Rabbit Production
en.short: Pig and rabbit housing, feeding, breeding, farrowing, kindling, health and feed conversion.

sections.heading: Pig housing and feeding
sections.text:
Pigs are monogastric (single-stomached), so they need concentrate feed rather than forage. House them in concrete-floored pens or on deep litter; a farrowing pen protects piglets from being crushed. Feed a balanced ration: an energy source such as maize, an oilseed meal for protein, and minerals, with clean water always available.

Swill (kitchen waste) can carry disease, and many countries restrict or ban it.

sections.heading: Breeding, farrowing and health
sections.text:
A gilt (a female before her first litter) is mated at her second or third oestrus; the cycle is about 21 days. Gestation averages 114 days, often remembered as three months, three weeks and three days. At farrowing (birth), provide bedding, warmth and a creep area the sow cannot enter.

Litters are commonly 8 to 12 piglets, weaned at 3 to 6 weeks. Stages run piglet, weaner, grower, finisher, then breeding stock. Herd health rests on quarantine, hygiene and culling sick animals.

sections.heading: Rabbit housing and breeding
sections.text:
Rabbits are monogastric hindgut fermenters that use forage well. Keep them in hutches or cages off the ground, shaded from sun and rain, with a nest box for the doe. Feed grass or legume hay plus a concentrate pellet.

They practise coprophagy, eating soft night faeces (caecotrophs) to recover protein and B vitamins. Does are induced ovulators: mating triggers ovulation. Gestation is about 31 days; kindling (birth) gives 4 to 10 kits, weaned at 4 to 6 weeks. Colony health rests on hygiene, space and quarantine.

sections.heading: Feed use and output
sections.text:
Pigs compete with people for grain, unlike ruminants fed on grass; rabbits, raised mainly on forage, compete less. Pigs grow faster and give heavier carcasses; rabbits give less meat each but thrive on forage and need little capital.

Compare them by feed conversion ratio (FCR): feed eaten divided by liveweight gain. If 10 weaners each gain 70 kg (700 kg total) and eat 2,100 kg of feed, FCR = 2,100 ÷ 700 = 3.0. At 75 per cent dressing (carcass share of liveweight), 700 × 0.75 = 525 kg carcass.

keyPoints: Pigs and rabbits are monogastric; pigs need concentrates, while rabbits use forage well as hindgut fermenters.
Pig gestation averages 114 days; rabbit gestation is about 31 days.
Farrowing pens and nest boxes protect the young; piglets are weaned at 3 to 6 weeks and kits at 4 to 6 weeks.
Rabbits are induced ovulators and practise coprophagy to recover nutrients.
Feed conversion ratio = feed eaten ÷ liveweight gain; use it to compare species, rations and pens.
Herd and colony health rest on quarantine of new stock, hygiene and culling of sick animals.

en.title: Livestock Housing and Farm Infrastructure
en.short: Site selection, ventilation, temperature, drainage, stocking density, waste handling and farm facilities.

sections.heading: Site selection and layout
sections.text: Pick a site that is well drained, gently sloping and above flood level, with road access, a reliable water source and room to expand. Keep housing away from homes and other farms as local regulations and biosecurity advice require, and place it so prevailing winds carry odour and dust away from people and clean areas. Plan separate clean and dirty routes, so feed and milk do not cross manure traffic.

sections.heading: Ventilation, temperature and drainage
sections.text: Ventilation replaces stale air and removes moisture, heat, dust and gases such as ammonia, while supplying oxygen. Natural ventilation uses open ridges and side openings; mechanical systems use fans and need power backup. Temperature control comes from orientation, insulation, shade, roof height and enough air space. Floors should slope to a channel so urine and wash water drain to a pit or lagoon, never to a stream.

sections.heading: Stocking density and waste
sections.text:
Stocking density is the floor area allowed per animal. Too little space raises heat, humidity and ammonia, increases aggression and spreads disease. Waste handling covers manure, slurry and dirty bedding: scrape or flush regularly, store in a covered pit, lagoon or compost heap away from water, and spread on land only at rates the soil and crops can use.

Worked example: a pen is 5 m × 4 m = 20 m². If the recommended allowance is 0.75 m² per growing pig, then 20 ÷ 0.75 = 26.7, so stock 26 pigs. Check: 26 × 0.75 = 19.5 m², which fits; 27 would need 20.25 m². Allowances vary with body weight and country, so check current guidelines.

sections.heading: Farm facilities
sections.text: Fencing marks boundaries and controls grazing: a perimeter fence, paddock subdivisions and, where used, electric strands. Water supply needs troughs sized for peak demand, cleaned often, with pipes protected from damage. A milking parlour should be separate from dung and dust, with a milk room and washable surfaces. A feed store should be dry, raised off the floor, ventilated and rodent-proof. Handling facilities, a race, crush and loading ramp, let animals be moved and restrained with less stress and injury.

keyPoints: Choose a drained, gently sloping site above flood level with water and road access.
Ventilation removes moisture, heat, ammonia and dust and supplies oxygen.
Slope floors to a channel and lead waste water to a pit or lagoon, not a stream.
Stocking density is floor area per animal; too little space harms health and growth.
Store manure away from water and spread it only at safe rates.
Good fencing, water, parlour, feed store and handling facilities cut stress and losses.

en.title: Pasture, Range and Grazing Management
en.short: Pasture establishment, fertiliser use, stocking rate, carrying capacity, rotational grazing, range management and rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Establishment and fertiliser
sections.text:
Pasture establishment means sowing or planting grasses and legumes for grazing or cutting. Match species to soil, rainfall and grazing system. Control weeds, test soil, use good seed, and sow at the right depth and season.

Grass-legume mixtures add protein; inoculate legume seed where rhizobia are absent. Fertilise from soil-test advice. Nitrogen boosts grasses; phosphorus and potassium support legumes and roots. Split nitrogen applications and avoid grazing wet, fertilised pasture. Manure can help but may spread weeds and parasites. Fertiliser rules vary by country; check guidance.

sections.heading: Stocking rate and capacity
sections.text:
Stocking rate is the number of animals on a unit of land for a stated period, often expressed as animals per hectare. Carrying capacity is the maximum stocking rate the land can support over time without degradation. It changes with rainfall, soil, species and management.

Estimate usable forage and divide by animal needs. Example: 10 hectares yield 30,000 kg of usable forage per year, and one animal needs 3,000 kg. Carrying capacity = 30,000 ÷ 3,000 = 10 animals. Stocking rate = 10 ÷ 10 = 1 animal per hectare. Keep a margin for drought.

sections.heading: Rotation and range
sections.text:
Rotational grazing moves animals between paddocks so each can rest and regrow. Rest lets leaves regrow, reserves rebuild and roots deepen. Set grazing periods by forage growth, not calendar alone.

Range management applies similar ideas to natural rangeland, which is usually not sown. It includes controlling animal numbers, placing water and salt away from sensitive areas, planned burning where appropriate, and bush clearing. Bush clearing removes unwanted woody plants by mechanical, chemical or biological means. Clear only where erosion risk is low, and check local rules before using chemicals.

sections.heading: Overgrazing and rehabilitation
sections.text:
Overgrazing is repeated heavy grazing that removes plants faster than they recover. It reduces ground cover, favours unpalatable species, compacts soil and causes erosion.

Rehabilitation starts by reducing grazing pressure. Then protect the area, control erosion, restore water infiltration, and reseed adapted species where needed. Monitor cover and species; recovery is slow.

keyPoints: Pasture establishment needs adapted species, good seed, weed control and soil-test-based fertiliser.
Stocking rate is animals per unit area; carrying capacity is the maximum sustainable stocking rate.
Carrying capacity = usable forage ÷ forage needed per animal; stocking rate = animals ÷ area.
Rotational grazing rests paddocks so plants recover and roots deepen.
Range management controls grazing, water, fire and bush encroachment on natural rangeland.
Overgrazing reduces cover and causes erosion; rehabilitation needs reduced grazing, protection and reseeding where needed.

en.title: Livestock Environment and Animal Welfare
en.short: Heat and cold stress, welfare signs, five freedoms, low-stress handling, and housing and transport rules.

sections.heading: Heat and cold stress
sections.text:
Heat stress occurs when an animal cannot lose enough heat to keep body temperature normal. High temperature, humidity, sun and poor air movement make it worse. Signs include panting, faster breathing, seeking shade, reduced feed intake, drooling and weakness. Pigs and poultry sweat little.

Cold stress occurs when heat loss exceeds heat production. Signs include shivering, huddling, hair or feather erection, cold extremities, poor growth and hypothermia. Young, thin and newly shorn animals lose heat fastest.

sections.heading: Signs of poor welfare
sections.text:
Poor welfare shows in behaviour, health and body condition. Watch for stereotypies (repeated purposeless actions such as bar-biting or feather pecking), tail biting, aggression, excessive fear, lameness, injuries, dirty coats, abnormal posture, low body condition, high mortality and poor growth. One sign is not proof; use records and repeated observation.

Example: a poultry house in Ogun State, Nigeria, with panting birds away from feeders and wet litter may have heat stress and poor ventilation. Check temperature, humidity, stocking density and water first.

sections.heading: Freedoms and handling
sections.text:
The widely taught Five Freedoms are freedom from hunger and thirst; from discomfort; from pain, injury and disease; from fear and distress; and freedom to express normal behaviour. Welfare science also considers mental state.

Low-stress handling uses the flight zone, the space that triggers an animal to move away, and the point of balance, usually at the shoulder. Move animals calmly in small groups, avoid shouting and electric prods, use non-slip flooring and trained handlers, and allow acclimatisation.

sections.heading: Housing and transport
sections.text:
Housing and transport standards protect welfare, but they differ by country. International guidelines come from WOAH (World Organisation for Animal Health); they are not law unless adopted nationally. National laws set space, ventilation, bedding, inspection and transport rules. For example, the UK Animal Welfare Act 2006 and EU transport Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 exist.

For transport, animals should be fit for the journey, loaded without injury, given adequate space, ventilation, water and rest, and unloaded promptly. Check current national law and official guidance.

keyPoints: Heat stress occurs when an animal cannot lose enough heat; signs include panting, shade seeking and reduced feed intake.
Cold stress occurs when heat loss exceeds heat production; signs include shivering, huddling and hypothermia.
Poor welfare signs include stereotypies, injuries, lameness, excessive fear, dirty coats and high mortality.
The Five Freedoms cover hunger and thirst, discomfort, pain and disease, fear and distress, and normal behaviour.
Low-stress handling uses the flight zone and point of balance, calm movement in small groups and trained handlers.
Housing and transport rules differ by country; check WOAH guidelines and current national law.

en.title: Meat Production, Slaughter and Meat Hygiene
en.short: Muscle to meat conversion, ageing, carcass yield and grading, slaughter hygiene, inspection and cold chain.

sections.heading: Conversion and ageing
sections.text: After slaughter, muscle becomes meat through glycolysis and rigor mortis. Glycolysis breaks glycogen to lactic acid, lowering pH. When energy runs out, actin and myosin lock as rigor mortis. If pH falls while the carcass is warm, pale, soft, exudative meat can result in pigs; chronic stress can cause dark, firm, dry meat.
