Ageing, or conditioning, holds meat chilled so natural enzymes tenderise it. Electrical stimulation can speed pH fall. The process is species and handling dependent.

sections.heading: Slaughter and hygiene
sections.text: Pre-slaughter handling should reduce stress: quiet movement, adequate water, rest, and no long fasting. Stress depletes glycogen and affects pH and quality. Animals must be stunned before bleeding in most commercial systems, and bleeding should be prompt and complete. Abattoir hygiene separates clean and dirty areas, uses potable water, cleans knives and equipment, and requires workers to wash hands. Good slaughter hygiene lowers contamination of the carcass.

sections.heading: Inspection and cold chain
sections.text: Meat inspection examines the live animal where possible, then the carcass and organs for disease and contamination. It looks for zoonoses (animal-to-human diseases) such as tuberculosis and cysticercosis, abscesses, parasites and faecal contamination. Condemned parts are removed. The cold chain keeps meat at chill temperatures, commonly near 0 to 4 degrees Celsius for fresh meat, or frozen for longer storage; exact rules vary by country. Temperature control slows bacterial growth. Common hazards are Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, Campylobacter, parasites and residues.

sections.heading: Yield and grading
sections.text: Carcass yield is often expressed as dressing percentage: hot carcass weight ÷ live weight × 100. For example, a 500 kg steer with a 275 kg hot carcass gives 275 ÷ 500 × 100 = 55 per cent. Carcass grading classifies carcasses by conformation and fat cover, and sometimes by weight and age; grids and names differ by country. Yield grades estimate saleable meat, while quality grades describe eating quality.

keyPoints: Muscle to meat conversion involves glycolysis, pH fall and rigor mortis.
Ageing tenderises meat through natural enzymes under controlled chilling.
Stress before slaughter affects glycogen, pH and meat quality.
Abattoir hygiene and prompt bleeding reduce carcass contamination.
Meat inspection looks for disease, contamination and zoonoses; the cold chain slows microbial growth.
Dressing percentage = hot carcass weight ÷ live weight × 100; grading systems vary by country.

en.title: Wool, Hides, Skins and Minor Animal Products
en.short: Structure and quality of wool and hair, hide and skin defects, curing, storage and marketing.

sections.heading: Wool and hair structure
sections.text: Wool is a keratin fibre with three layers. The cuticle is the outer layer of overlapping scales. The cortex is the main body; in crimped wool it has ortho and para sections. The medulla is a central core of cells and air spaces, absent in fine wool and common in coarser fibres. Crimp means waves along the staple, a lock of fibres. Hair from goats, camels and similar animals often has a medulla, less crimp and a different scale pattern.

sections.heading: Quality and defects
sections.text: Wool quality is judged by fibre diameter (fineness), staple length, crimp, strength, colour, uniformity and clean yield. Clean yield is clean wool after removing grease, suint (sheep sweat) and dirt, divided by greasy weight. Kemp, a coarse medullated fibre, and vegetable matter lower value. Hides are from cattle; skins from smaller animals. Defects include flay cuts, holes, scars, brand marks, tick and warble damage, putrefaction, hair slip and salt burn. They lower the grain (outer surface) grade and leather value.

sections.heading: Handling, curing, storage
sections.text: Flay promptly and carefully, remove flesh and fat, and cool the hide or skin. Curing preserves it before tanning. Common methods are salting, drying and pickling with salt and acid; chilling is short-term. Never stack warm, wet hides. Store cured stock cool, dry, off the ground, with insect and rodent control. By-products such as blood, bone, horns, hooves, tallow, lanolin and manure need quick, clean collection and separate storage.

sections.heading: Marketing and example
sections.text: Fibre is classed and sold by objective measurements, often through auctions or cooperatives. Hides and skins are graded by area, thickness and defects, then sold to tanneries or exporters. Minor products may be sold locally or processed further. Prices and regulations vary by country; check current grading rules and export requirements. Example: a 4.0 kg greasy fleece yields 2.4 kg clean wool. Clean yield = (2.4 ÷ 4.0) × 100 = 60%. For 1,000 such fleeces, clean wool = 1,000 × 2.4 = 2,400 kg.

keyPoints: Wool has a cuticle, cortex and sometimes a medulla; fine wool lacks a medulla.
Wool quality depends on fibre diameter, staple length, crimp, strength, colour and clean yield.
Clean yield (%) = clean wool weight ÷ greasy wool weight × 100.
Hides and skins are graded down by cuts, scars, parasite damage, putrefaction and salt burn.
Cure hides and skins promptly by salting, drying or pickling, then store cool and dry.
Marketing depends on grading; prices and regulations vary by country, so check current official rules.

en.title: Livestock Economics, Farm Records and Budgets
en.short: Budgets, gross margins, costs, break-even and herd records for judging livestock enterprises.

sections.heading: Costs and gross margin
sections.text: Variable costs change with the number of animals or level of output: feed, drugs, casual labour, transport. Fixed costs do not change in the short run: land rent, buildings, equipment, permanent labour. Gross margin is gross output (sales plus value of stock change) minus variable costs. It measures what an enterprise contributes towards fixed costs and profit. A positive gross margin covers variable costs but does not prove profit.

sections.heading: Enterprise budget
sections.text: An enterprise budget is a planned statement for one enterprise, such as a broiler flock, for a stated period. List expected output and its value, then variable costs, giving the gross margin. Subtract fixed costs to get profit. Use consistent units, for example per bird, per sow per year, or per hectare, so enterprises can be compared. Budgets are estimates; check prices and yields locally.

sections.heading: Break-even example
sections.text:
Break-even output is the level at which total revenue equals total costs. For one product:
break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit).
The bracket is the contribution per unit. Suppose a pig enterprise has fixed costs of 120,000 per year, a sale price of 30,000 per pig and variable cost of 18,000 per pig. Contribution = 12,000. Break-even = 120,000 ÷ 12,000 = 10 pigs per year. At 12 pigs, profit = (12 × 12,000) − 120,000 = 24,000. Check: revenue 360,000, variable costs 216,000, gross margin 144,000, less fixed costs 120,000 = 24,000.

sections.heading: Records and judgement
sections.text: Keep breeding, birth, death, feed, health, milk or egg yield, sales and costs records for each herd or flock. Identify animals by tag or ear notch, and record events when they happen. From records calculate performance: feed conversion, mortality, weaning rate, cost per litre or per egg. An enterprise pays if its gross margin is positive and covers its share of fixed costs, and if returns exceed the next best use of land, labour and capital. Compare over several periods, not one season.

keyPoints: Variable costs change with output; fixed costs do not change in the short run.
Gross margin = gross output − variable costs.
Enterprise budget profit = gross output − variable costs − fixed costs.
Break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit).
Keep individual animal and flock records for breeding, health, feed, yield and costs.
An enterprise pays if its gross margin covers fixed costs and its returns beat the next best use of resources.

en.title: Livestock Marketing, Trade and Cooperatives
en.short: Livestock markets, price formation, middlemen, transport, cooperatives, contracts and standards.

sections.heading: Markets and price formation
sections.text:
A livestock market is any place or arrangement where live animals or animal products change hands. It may be a physical market, auction, farm gate sale or digital listing.

Price is formed by supply and demand, but quality matters: species, weight, age, breed, health and uniformity. Season, feed costs, disease, transport cost and market information also shift price. Sellers with better information and more buyers bargain better. Prices differ by country and year, so check current market reports.

sections.heading: Middlemen and transport
sections.text:
Middlemen include brokers, assemblers, wholesalers and retailers. They connect scattered farms to buyers, provide credit, bear risk and arrange transport. They can take a large margin when competition is weak, so farmers should compare offers.

Transport affects marketing directly. Animals lose weight and may be stressed or injured, and disease can spread. Good practice uses suitable vehicles, careful loading, water, rest and required veterinary certificates. Trade ranges from local to international, and movement and import rules vary by country.

sections.heading: Cooperatives and contracts
sections.text:
A cooperative is a business owned and controlled by its members. In livestock marketing, members may pool sales, buy feed and drugs in bulk, share transport and negotiate with buyers.

A contract is a binding agreement, usually written, covering quantity, quality, price, delivery and payment. Contracts reduce price risk, but need clear terms, realistic delivery dates and a way to settle disputes. Standards are agreed rules on grades, weights, hygiene, animal health and traceability. Public standards are set by government; private standards by buyers or schemes. They help buyers trust what they receive.

sections.heading: Case and check
sections.text:
Suppose Amina in northern Nigeria sells goats. A broker offers one flat price per goat. Her cooperative weighs and grades the goats, finds several buyers, arranges transport and signs a supply contract. It deducts a small levy. Amina compares her net receipt, not just the headline price.

Open accounts and member control keep the cooperative honest. Check current national rules on animal movement, veterinary certificates and cooperative registration.

keyPoints: A livestock market is any arrangement where animals or products change hands, not only a physical market.
Price reflects supply, demand, quality, weight, health, season, costs and market information.
Middlemen provide assembly, credit, risk bearing and transport, but weak competition can raise their margins.
Transport causes weight loss, stress, injury and disease spread, so loading, water, rest and veterinary checks matter.
Cooperatives pool sales and purchases and strengthen bargaining, but need open accounts and member control.
Contracts and standards reduce risk and build buyer trust, while movement and trade rules vary by country.

en.title: Animal Production Ethics, Law and Professional Practice
en.short: Honest records and sales, animal care, consumer duties, and Nigerian regulators.

sections.heading: Professional ethics
sections.text:
Professional ethics are the standards of conduct expected of trained animal scientists and veterinarians. They include honesty, competence, confidentiality and avoiding conflicts of interest.

A conflict of interest is when a personal gain could sway a professional judgement, such as a veterinarian selling a drug in which they have a financial stake. Ethical practice means putting animal health and public safety before profit.

sections.heading: Records and sales
sections.text:
Farm records must be accurate and complete. They cover animal identity, births, deaths, treatments, withdrawal periods and sales. A withdrawal period is the time after a medicine is given before meat, milk or eggs may be sold.

Falsifying a record is dishonest and can lead to drug residues in food. In sales, do not misrepresent age, breed, pregnancy, health or treatment history. If Amina knows her heifer is not pregnant, saying she is pregnant is fraud. Disclose defects and record the sale truthfully.

sections.heading: Care and consumers
sections.text:
Care of animals means meeting their needs for feed, water, space, health care and humane handling. Neglect and cruel handling are unprofessional even where the law is weak.

Responsibility to consumers means supplying safe, wholesome food and truthful information. Do not sell diseased animals or milk from treated cows before the withdrawal period ends. Traceability, meaning the ability to follow an animal or product through the chain, supports recalls and honest claims.

sections.heading: Nigerian regulators
sections.text:
In Nigeria, the Veterinary Council of Nigeria (VCN) regulates veterinary practice. The Nigerian Institute of Animal Science (NIAS) regulates the animal science profession, registering practitioners and setting standards of conduct. The federal agriculture ministry (currently the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security), with state veterinary services, oversees animal health and disease control.

The Nigeria Agricultural Quarantine Service (NAQS) controls agricultural quarantine, including imports and exports of animals and animal products. The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) regulates veterinary drugs and food safety, and the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) sets product standards. These bodies’ rules, and the ministries they sit under, change, so check current official sources.

keyPoints: Professional ethics put animal health and public safety before profit.
Keep accurate records of identity, treatments, withdrawal periods and sales.
Never misrepresent an animal’s health, pregnancy, age or treatment in a sale.
Meet animals’ needs and handle them humanely.
Consumers deserve safe food and truthful information, so respect withdrawal periods.
In Nigeria, NIAS, VCN, NAQS, NAFDAC and SON have regulatory roles, and their rules change.

en.title: Research Methods and the Final Project in Animal Science
en.short: Covers framing questions, literature review, trial and survey design, sample size, analysis, ethics and report writing.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text:
A research question states what you will find out. It must be answerable with the animals, time and money available. Name the population, variables and comparison. For example: does adding a local legume to a maize-based diet change daily gain in growing pigs? A hypothesis turns this into a testable prediction.

The literature review shows what is known, identifies gaps and sharpens the question. Use primary sources, record search terms, and summarise by theme.

sections.heading: Trials and surveys
sections.text:
In a trial, compare treatments. Use random allocation, a control where ethical, replication and, where possible, blocking to reduce nuisance variation. Keep management the same except the treatment.

In a survey, define the target population and the sampling frame (the list you will sample from), then use probability sampling such as simple random sampling. Pilot the questionnaire to test wording and recording. Avoid leading questions and non-response bias.

sections.heading: Sample size and analysis
sections.text:
Sample size depends on the question, design, variability, confidence and power. For a survey proportion, n = Z² p(1−p) ÷ e². With 95% confidence Z = 1.96, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05: n = 1.96² × 0.25 ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so 385. For N = 1,000, adjust: n = 385 ÷ (1 + 384 ÷ 1,000) = 278.2, so 279.

Analyse with methods that match the design. Start with descriptive statistics and graphs, check assumptions, then use confidence intervals and suitable tests. Do not change the planned analysis after seeing results without saying so.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text:
Get approval from your institution’s ethics committee before collecting data. For animal work, follow local animal welfare law and committee rules; apply the 3Rs: replacement, reduction and refinement. Obtain informed consent for human participants, protect confidentiality and store data securely. Never fabricate or falsify results.

Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words, ideas or data as your own. Cite every source, quote direct words, paraphrase properly and list full references. Check your institution’s policy. Write the report in the standard order: abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references.

keyPoints: A research question must name the population, variables and comparison, and be answerable with available resources.
The literature review identifies gaps; use primary sources and record search terms.
Trials need random allocation, controls where ethical, replication and blocking; surveys need a sampling frame and probability sampling.
For a survey proportion, n = Z² p(1−p) ÷ e²; adjust for a finite population with n = n0 ÷ (1 + (n0 − 1) ÷ N).
Match analysis to design; start descriptive, check assumptions, then use confidence intervals and suitable tests.
Get ethics approval, apply the 3Rs in animal work, never fabricate data, and cite all sources to avoid plagiarism.

en.title: Advanced Animal Genetics and Genomics
en.short: Quantitative models, BLUP breeding values, genomic selection, G×E and breeding scheme design.

sections.heading: Quantitative models
sections.text: Quantitative genetics treats a phenotype P as the sum of an additive breeding value A, dominance D, epistasis I and environment E: P = A + D + I + E. Only A is passed reliably to offspring, so breeding value is the main target. The additive genetic variance σ²A and phenotypic variance σ²P give heritability h² = σ²A ÷ σ²P. REML (restricted maximum likelihood) estimates variance components.

sections.heading: Mixed models and example
sections.text: A mixed model writes records as y = Xb + Zu + e. Here b holds fixed effects such as herd, sex or age; u holds random breeding values; X and Z are design matrices; e is residual error. The mixed model equations solve b and u together, and the solution for u is the best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP). Example: if h² = 0.4 and an animal is 10 kg above its herd mean, its simple EBV is 0.4 × 10 = 4 kg. More relatives and records raise accuracy.

sections.heading: Markers and genomic selection
sections.text: Molecular markers are DNA variants, commonly single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), used to trace chromosome segments. A marker linked to a quantitative trait locus (QTL) can aid selection, but effects are often small. Genomic selection uses many markers at once. A reference population with genotypes and phenotypes trains a prediction model; candidates are then ranked by genomic estimated breeding values (GEBV). A genomic relationship matrix can replace pedigree in BLUP. Genomic selection helps for sex-limited or late-measured traits, but predictions need validation in the target population.

sections.heading: G×E and scheme design
sections.text: Genotype by environment interaction (G×E) means genotypes rank differently across environments. It can be modelled with reaction norms (a genotype’s performance pattern across environments) or by estimating genetic correlations between environments; a low correlation implies separate breeding programmes may be justified. A genetic improvement scheme should define the breeding objective, record phenotypes, choose selection criteria, use AI or embryo transfer, control inbreeding, and disseminate improved stock through nucleus and multiplier tiers. Genomic selection shortens intervals. Schemes vary by country, so check national rules.

keyPoints: Phenotype decomposes as P = A + D + I + E, and only additive breeding value A is inherited reliably.
Heritability is h² = σ²A ÷ σ²P; REML estimates variance components.
The mixed model y = Xb + Zu + e gives BLUP breeding values by solving the mixed model equations.
For one own record, EBV = h²(y − herd mean); more records and relatives raise accuracy.
Genomic selection trains on a reference population and predicts GEBV from many markers; validate before use.
G×E means re-ranking across environments; design schemes with clear objectives, recording, inbreeding control and dissemination.

en.title: Advanced Ruminant and Monogastric Nutrition
en.short: Rumen fermentation, energy and protein systems, lipids, methane and nutrient modelling.

sections.heading: Rumen fermentation
sections.text: Rumen fermentation is anaerobic. Bacteria, protozoa, fungi and archaea break down feed, converting carbohydrates mainly to volatile fatty acids (VFAs): acetate, propionate and butyrate, plus gases. Fibre ferments slowly and favours acetate; starch ferments quickly and can lower pH. Microbes build microbial protein from ammonia, peptides and amino acids, but energy and nitrogen must be available together. Methanogenic archaea combine hydrogen with carbon dioxide to form methane, an energy loss. Monogastric animals lack a rumen; enzymatic digestion dominates, with some hindgut fermentation.

sections.heading: Energy and methane
sections.text: Energy systems move from gross energy (GE) to digestible energy (DE), metabolisable energy (ME) and net energy (NE). ME = DE − methane energy − urine energy. NE = ME × k, where k is efficiency of use and varies with diet and production. Methane is an energy loss and an environmental cost. Example: GE 18 MJ/kg dry matter (DM), DE 14, methane 1.2 and urine 0.8 MJ/kg DM. ME = 14 − 1.2 − 0.8 = 12.0 MJ/kg DM. If k = 0.60, NE = 12.0 × 0.60 = 7.2 MJ/kg DM. 14 − 2.0 = 12.0; 12.0 × 0.60 = 7.2.

sections.heading: Amino acids and lipids
sections.text: Ruminants absorb metabolisable protein (MP), microbial protein plus digestible rumen-undegraded protein (RUP). RUP and protected amino acids can correct limiting amino acids. Monogastric animals need essential amino acids; assess supply as ileal digestible amino acids against an ideal profile. Lipids are concentrated energy. Ruminants biohydrogenate unsaturated fatty acids in the rumen, converting them to more saturated forms; protected fats raise energy density, but excess fat can depress fibre digestion. Monogastric animals require linoleic acid; alpha-linolenic acid is important in some species.

sections.heading: Modelling supply and requirement
sections.text: Nutrient models compare predicted supply with factorial requirements. Requirements are summed for maintenance, growth, lactation or reproduction. Supply is predicted from intake, digestion, absorption and, in ruminants, rumen fermentation and microbial protein. Mechanistic models simulate the rumen; empirical models fit equations. Outputs depend on feed data and validation. Use local feed analyses, test sensitivity, and check predictions against animal performance.

keyPoints: Rumen microbes ferment feed to VFAs and microbial protein, and methanogens produce methane as an energy loss.
ME = DE − methane energy − urine energy; NE = ME × k, where k varies with diet and production.
In ruminants, metabolisable protein is supplied mainly by microbial protein plus digestible rumen-undegraded protein.
Monogastric amino acid supply is best assessed as ileal digestible essential amino acids against an ideal profile.
Ruminant lipids undergo biohydrogenation; protected fats can raise energy density but excess fat may depress fibre digestion.
Nutrient models compare predicted supply with factorial requirements and must be validated with local feed data.

en.title: Advanced Reproductive Biotechnology
en.short: Embryo transfer at scale, IVEP, freezing semen and embryos, cloning, stem cells and welfare limits.

sections.heading: Embryo transfer at scale
sections.text: Embryo transfer (ET) collects embryos from a donor and places them in synchronised recipients. It needs donor selection, superovulation (hormone-stimulated multiple ovulation), insemination with a chosen sire, non-surgical flushing, embryo grading and transfer to recipients at the same stage. Throughput depends on donor response, embryo quality and recipient supply. If 100 donors yield 6 transferable embryos each, that is 600 embryos; at a hypothetical 50% pregnancy rate, 300 pregnancies result.

sections.heading: IVEP and cryopreservation
sections.text: In vitro embryo production (IVEP) makes embryos outside the body. Oocytes are collected by ovum pick-up (OPU) from live donors or harvested from abattoir ovaries, then matured (IVM), fertilised (IVF) and cultured (IVC) to blastocyst, the early embryo stage. IVEP lets one sire serve many donors, but oocyte quality limits yield. Cryopreservation stores cells at very low temperature. Semen is extended, cooled, treated with cryoprotectants (freeze-protecting solutes) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Embryos are slow-frozen or vitrified (very rapid cooling without ice). Bull semen freezes better than boar semen.

sections.heading: Cloning and stem cells
sections.text: Cloning by somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) places a body cell nucleus into an enucleated oocyte (nucleus removed), activates it, cultures it to embryo and transfers it. It copies nuclear genes, not the whole animal. Stem cells are unspecialised cells that self-renew and can form several cell types. Embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells are studied in reproduction and medicine, but livestock applications remain experimental.

sections.heading: Physiology and welfare limits
sections.text: These methods work within physiology. Superovulation gives variable and declining responses, IVEP embryos are often less viable than in vivo ones, freezing damages some cells, and SCNT clones show high pregnancy loss and abnormalities. Welfare concerns include repeated hormone injections, surgery, OPU and abnormal clone development. Rules differ by country, so check the national veterinary authority before applying these methods.

keyPoints: ET requires a superovulated donor, good embryos and synchronised recipients.
IVEP uses OPU, IVM, IVF and IVC to blastocyst.
Cryoprotectants protect cells during freezing; embryos may be vitrified.
SCNT copies nuclear genes, not the whole animal.
Cloning and stem cell work in livestock remain inefficient and experimental.
Welfare and legal rules vary by country; check the national authority.

en.title: Livestock Systems Modelling and the Dissertation
en.short: Whole-farm and herd models, livestock LCA, shock analysis and the dissertation.

sections.heading: Whole-farm and herd models
sections.text: Whole-farm models represent the farm as connected parts: land, feed, animals, labour, money and outputs. Herd models track age and sex classes, births, deaths, culling, sales and replacements over time. Both are simplifications, so state assumptions, validate against farm records, and test key parameters with sensitivity analysis. They help compare feeding, breeding or selling plans before money is spent.

sections.heading: LCA and shocks
sections.text:
Life cycle assessment (LCA) estimates environmental burdens per functional unit, such as 1 kg of milk or 1 kg of live weight. It has four stages: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment and interpretation. The system boundary decides which stages count, and allocation divides burdens between milk and meat. A simple inventory calculation is activity data × emission factor. If feed use is 10,000 kg and the factor is 0.5 kg CO2e (carbon dioxide equivalent) per kg, feed emissions are 5,000 kg CO2e. The factor is illustrative; use verified local factors.

Climate and market shocks are tested by scenario and sensitivity analysis. A drought may cut feed supply and conception; a feed price rise raises costs. In a herd model with 100 cows and 20% culling, 20 cows leave and 80 remain. Keeping 100 needs 20 replacements. If drought leaves only 10 heifers, the herd falls to 90 unless 10 are bought.

sections.heading: Dissertation craft
sections.text: For the dissertation, turn a practical problem into a focused question and a written protocol. Plan ethics approval, data management and a timeline early. Choose statistics that match the design: regression for continuous outcomes, analysis of variance for group means, and survival analysis for time to event. Report estimates with uncertainty, not only p values. In writing, make the methods reproducible, keep results factual, and use the discussion to compare findings with published work and state limits. Edit for plain English and check every table and reference.

keyPoints: A whole-farm model links feed, animals, money and outputs; a herd model tracks births, deaths, culling and sales over time.
LCA reports impacts per functional unit and depends on system boundary and allocation choices.
Inventory emissions = activity data × emission factor.
Herd change = births + purchases − deaths − sales − culling.
Scenario analysis tests climate or market shocks; sensitivity analysis shows which assumptions matter.
Match the statistical method to the design, report uncertainty, and write reproducible methods.
